breadcrumb: Program Overview/Program Considerations
recommendation_text: The Program strives towards equitable and safe delivery, particularly for populations disproportionately affected by structural factors such as targeted tobacco marketing, systemic healthcare access barriers and unequal access to cessation supports, which contributes to increased risk of lung cancer related to smoking prevalence [1, 20, 21, 22].

recommendation_text: Participation rates and significant rates of positive results requiring further investigation indicate that other cancer screening programs are not equitably meeting the needs of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people [21, 23, 24].

source_section: Program Overview/Program Considerations

breadcrumb: Program Overview/Program Considerations
recommendation_text: To help ensure the Program is culturally safe, the Australian Government is committed to working in partnership with Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples, communities and organisations [25, 26, 27].
source_name: Program Guidelines for the National Lung Cancer Screening Program: Targeted Lung Cancer Screening in High‐Risk Individuals in Australia
source_section: Program Overview/Program Considerations

breadcrumb: Program Overview/Program Considerations
recommendation_text: Stigma related to smoking can negatively impact how people who smoke or have a history of smoking engage with lung cancer screening, underscoring the importance of culturally safe, empathic and non‐judgemental care and communication—everyone deserves care, support and understanding [28].
source_name: Program Guidelines for the National Lung Cancer Screening Program: Targeted Lung Cancer Screening in High‐Risk Individuals in Australia
source_section: Program Overview/Program Considerations

breadcrumb: Program Overview/Program Considerations
recommendation_text: Given tobacco use is the single greatest avoidable risk factor for lung cancer [29], smoking cessation is an important component of any effective and equitable lung cancer screening program.

breadcrumb: Program Overview/Roles and Responsibilities Across the Program
recommendation_text: The Program is delivered across primary and tertiary care settings. All healthcare providers and health support workers may contribute to Program delivery.

breadcrumb: Program Overview/Roles and Responsibilities Across the Program
recommendation_text: Healthcare providers authorised to request low‐dose CT scans as part of the Program include general practitioners, medical specialists and nurse practitioners, and are referred to as ‘requesting practitioners’.

source_section: Program Overview/Roles and Responsibilities Across the Program

recommendation_text: Nurse practitioners are permitted to request program‐specific MBS items where state or territory legislation allows, following amendments to the Health Insurance Act 1973 (Cth) [30].

source_section: Program Overview/Roles and Responsibilities Across the Program

breadcrumb: Program Overview/Roles and Responsibilities Across the Program
recommendation_text: Radiology providers are responsible for reading and reporting the low‐dose CT scans, and communicating scan outcomes to requesting practitioners and the National Cancer Screening Register (NCSR). The NCSR provides a single electronic record for individuals participating in the lung, cervical and bowel cancer screening programs.
source_name: Program Guidelines for the National Lung Cancer Screening Program: Targeted Lung Cancer Screening in High‐Risk Individuals in Australia

breadcrumb: Recommendations
recommendation_text: The Program's guidelines comprise eight evidence‐based recommendations and 74 practice points for program delivery [19]. Recommendations are those supported by the MSAC expert advice on lung cancer screening, and additional items supported by evidence from systematic reviews and randomised controlled trials.
source_name: Program Guidelines for the National Lung Cancer Screening Program: Targeted Lung Cancer Screening in High‐Risk Individuals in Australia
source_section: Recommendations

breadcrumb: Recommendations
recommendation_text: Practice points provide guidance on delivery and implementation at each step of the screening and assessment pathway where issues are not addressed by other standards or guidelines, or where evidence is limited.

source_section: Recommendations

breadcrumb: Recommendations/Target Population and Eligibility Criteria
recommendation_text: The Program targets individuals at high risk of lung cancer to ensure the program is safe and effective. Eligibility is based on risk criteria recommended by MSAC [15]. To participate, individuals must meet all four criteria: Aged 50 to 70 years; Asymptomatic (no signs or symptoms suggestive of lung cancer);
source_name: Program Guidelines for the National Lung Cancer Screening Program: Targeted Lung Cancer Screening in High‐Risk Individuals in Australia
source_section: Recommendations/Target Population and Eligibility Criteria

breadcrumb: Recommendations/Target Population and Eligibility Criteria
recommendation_text: Currently smoke or have quit smoking within the past 10 years; andHave a history of at least 30 pack‐years of tobacco cigarette smoking.
source_name: Program Guidelines for the National Lung Cancer Screening Program: Targeted Lung Cancer Screening in High‐Risk Individuals in Australia
source_section: Recommendations/Target Population and Eligibility Criteria

breadcrumb: Recommendations/Smoking Cessation
recommendation_text: Smoking cessation supports are to be offered, where appropriate, to all potential participants by healthcare providers across the screening and assessment pathway; this includes follow‐up and maintenance support.
source_name: Program Guidelines for the National Lung Cancer Screening Program: Targeted Lung Cancer Screening in High‐Risk Individuals in Australia
source_section: Recommendations/Smoking Cessation

breadcrumb: Recommendations/Smoking Cessation
recommendation_text: Evidence from trials demonstrate that lung cancer screening participants have higher quit rates than rates expected in the general smoking population [31]. Support to quit smoking or maintain cessation is strongly recommended to be delivered using the three‐step brief intervention model ‘Ask, Advise, Help’ [32, 33].
source_name: Program Guidelines for the National Lung Cancer Screening Program: Targeted Lung Cancer Screening in High‐Risk Individuals in Australia
source_section: Recommendations/Smoking Cessation

breadcrumb: Recommendations/Smoking Cessation
recommendation_text: People who smoke may choose brief advice, pharmacotherapy, referral to local services, Quitline or no further support at this time. Cessation medicines, including varenicline and bupropion, are subsidised on the Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme, and can be accessed with a prescription.
source_name: Program Guidelines for the National Lung Cancer Screening Program: Targeted Lung Cancer Screening in High‐Risk Individuals in Australia
source_section: Recommendations/Smoking Cessation

breadcrumb: Recommendations/Smoking Cessation
recommendation_text: The requesting practitioner can help to arrange a referral to multi‐session behavioural interventions. All options should be offered without pressure or stigma. People who smoke do not have to quit smoking to participate in the Program.
source_name: Program Guidelines for the National Lung Cancer Screening Program: Targeted Lung Cancer Screening in High‐Risk Individuals in Australia
source_section: Recommendations/Smoking Cessation

breadcrumb: Recommendations/Low‐Dose CT Scan Assessment and Reporting
recommendation_text: The Program uses a nationally standardised approach for scan assessment and reporting.
source_name: Program Guidelines for the National Lung Cancer Screening Program: Targeted Lung Cancer Screening in High‐Risk Individuals in Australia
source_section: Recommendations/Low‐Dose CT Scan Assessment and Reporting

breadcrumb: Recommendations/Low‐Dose CT Scan Assessment and Reporting
recommendation_text: Baseline screening scans and follow‐up scans are read and reported using the Program's nodule management protocol [34], developed by the Australian Government in collaboration with the Australian and New Zealand Society of Thoracic Radiology (ANZSTR, for the Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Radiologists [RANZCR]) and the Thoracic Society
source_name: Program Guidelines for the National Lung Cancer Screening Program: Targeted Lung Cancer Screening in High‐Risk Individuals in Australia
source_section: Recommendations/Low‐Dose CT Scan Assessment and Reporting

breadcrumb: Recommendations/Low‐Dose CT Scan Assessment and Reporting
recommendation_text: The protocol was developed to support MSAC's recommendation to use the Pan‐Canadian Early Detection of Lung Cancer Study (PanCan) nodule malignancy risk calculator [35] and the Lung CT Screening Reporting and Data System (Lung‐RADS) [36], adapted for the Australian context with a biennial screening interval.
source_name: Program Guidelines for the National Lung Cancer Screening Program: Targeted Lung Cancer Screening in High‐Risk Individuals in Australia
source_section: Recommendations/Low‐Dose CT Scan Assessment and Reporting

breadcrumb: Recommendations/Low‐Dose CT Scan Assessment and Reporting
recommendation_text: Radiologists are required to report all Program low‐dose CT scan results to the NCSR using the Program's structured clinical radiology report.
source_name: Program Guidelines for the National Lung Cancer Screening Program: Targeted Lung Cancer Screening in High‐Risk Individuals in Australia
source_section: Recommendations/Low‐Dose CT Scan Assessment and Reporting

breadcrumb: Summary of the Lung Cancer Screening and Assessment Pathway
recommendation_text: The lung cancer screening and assessment pathway defines clinical and policy parameters and maps the participant journey. Key components of the pathway (Figure 1) are summarised in the following paragraphs.

source_section: Summary of the Lung Cancer Screening and Assessment Pathway

breadcrumb: Summary of the Lung Cancer Screening and Assessment Pathway/Promotion and Awareness
recommendation_text: Widespread, repeated promotion is important to maximise participation in the Program. Governments, service providers and healthcare professionals share responsibility for proactively raising awareness among eligible individuals and the broader community. Healthcare providers play a key role in recommending screening and disseminating information.
source_name: Program Guidelines for the National Lung Cancer Screening Program: Targeted Lung Cancer Screening in High‐Risk Individuals in Australia
source_section: Summary of the Lung Cancer Screening and Assessment Pathway/Promotion and Awareness

breadcrumb: Summary of the Lung Cancer Screening and Assessment Pathway/Promotion and Awareness
recommendation_text: International evidence shows that lack of awareness and understanding of screening benefits are major barriers to participation [37, 38, 39]. Practice points emphasise promoting the Program in culturally safe, appropriate and accessible ways that consider varying levels of literacy and health literacy and address stigma.
source_name: Program Guidelines for the National Lung Cancer Screening Program: Targeted Lung Cancer Screening in High‐Risk Individuals in Australia
source_section: Summary of the Lung Cancer Screening and Assessment Pathway/Promotion and Awareness

breadcrumb: Summary of the Lung Cancer Screening and Assessment Pathway/Program Entry and Recruitment
recommendation_text: Recruitment involves identifying and engaging individuals at high risk of lung cancer to participate in the Program, occurring across multiple settings. Unlike population‐based cancer screening programs for bowel, breast and cervical cancer, the Program does not issue invitations to potential participants.
source_name: Program Guidelines for the National Lung Cancer Screening Program: Targeted Lung Cancer Screening in High‐Risk Individuals in Australia
source_section: Summary of the Lung Cancer Screening and Assessment Pathway/Program Entry and Recruitment

breadcrumb: Summary of the Lung Cancer Screening and Assessment Pathway/Program Entry and Recruitment
recommendation_text: As a targeted screening program with risk‐based eligibility criteria, eligibility cannot be determined solely by age, and information about smoking history is not contained in government registers such as Medicare. Potential participants may enrol in the Program via four routes: organised, opportunistic, facilitated or self‐identified entry.
source_name: Program Guidelines for the National Lung Cancer Screening Program: Targeted Lung Cancer Screening in High‐Risk Individuals in Australia
source_section: Summary of the Lung Cancer Screening and Assessment Pathway/Program Entry and Recruitment

breadcrumb: Summary of the Lung Cancer Screening and Assessment Pathway/Program Entry and Recruitment
recommendation_text: Each route requires eligibility assessment and a low‐dose CT scan request by a requesting practitioner. Enrolled participants receive a welcome pack from the NCSR.
source_name: Program Guidelines for the National Lung Cancer Screening Program: Targeted Lung Cancer Screening in High‐Risk Individuals in Australia
source_section: Summary of the Lung Cancer Screening and Assessment Pathway/Program Entry and Recruitment

breadcrumb: Summary of the Lung Cancer Screening and Assessment Pathway/Program Entry and Recruitment
recommendation_text: Practice points highlight strategies to optimise access and support recruitment by leveraging electronic medical records (EMRs) to facilitate participant recruitment, such as updating smoking history records, conducting EMR audits and using EMR‐based prompts.
source_name: Program Guidelines for the National Lung Cancer Screening Program: Targeted Lung Cancer Screening in High‐Risk Individuals in Australia
source_section: Summary of the Lung Cancer Screening and Assessment Pathway/Program Entry and Recruitment

breadcrumb: Summary of the Lung Cancer Screening and Assessment Pathway/Eligibility and Low‐Dose CT Scan Request
recommendation_text: A wide range of healthcare providers may discuss and check if people are eligible to participate in the Program. Eligibility should be confirmed by a requesting practitioner. There are no program‐specific MBS items for the eligibility assessment. Existing MBS items for short and long consultations can be used.
source_name: Program Guidelines for the National Lung Cancer Screening Program: Targeted Lung Cancer Screening in High‐Risk Individuals in Australia
source_section: Summary of the Lung Cancer Screening and Assessment Pathway/Eligibility and Low‐Dose CT Scan Request

breadcrumb: Summary of the Lung Cancer Screening and Assessment Pathway/Eligibility and Low‐Dose CT Scan Request
recommendation_text: Participants must be aged between 50 and 70 years, and have no signs or symptoms suggestive of lung cancer, to remain eligible. Enrolled participants do not need their smoking history eligibility criteria reassessed for subsequent scan requests.
source_name: Program Guidelines for the National Lung Cancer Screening Program: Targeted Lung Cancer Screening in High‐Risk Individuals in Australia
source_section: Summary of the Lung Cancer Screening and Assessment Pathway/Eligibility and Low‐Dose CT Scan Request

breadcrumb: Summary of the Lung Cancer Screening and Assessment Pathway/Eligibility and Low‐Dose CT Scan Request
recommendation_text: Practice points guide healthcare providers in calculating smoking pack‐year history, enrolling eligible individuals into the Program and reassessing eligibility for those who may become eligible over time due to ageing or increased pack‐years of smoking.
source_name: Program Guidelines for the National Lung Cancer Screening Program: Targeted Lung Cancer Screening in High‐Risk Individuals in Australia
source_section: Summary of the Lung Cancer Screening and Assessment Pathway/Eligibility and Low‐Dose CT Scan Request

breadcrumb: Summary of the Lung Cancer Screening and Assessment Pathway/Eligibility and Low‐Dose CT Scan Request/Suitability for Low‐Dose CT
recommendation_text: Requesting practitioners must check suitability for low‐dose CT before completing each low‐dose CT scan request. Requesting practitioners should consider an individual's general health and ability to physically use CT scanners.
source_name: Program Guidelines for the National Lung Cancer Screening Program: Targeted Lung Cancer Screening in High‐Risk Individuals in Australia
source_section: Summary of the Lung Cancer Screening and Assessment Pathway/Eligibility and Low‐Dose CT Scan Request/Suitability for Low‐Dose CT

breadcrumb: Summary of the Lung Cancer Screening and Assessment Pathway/Eligibility and Low‐Dose CT Scan Request/Suitability for Low‐Dose CT
recommendation_text: If an eligible person has health reasons that make low‐dose CT clinically inappropriate, these should be managed as per usual care arrangements.
source_name: Program Guidelines for the National Lung Cancer Screening Program: Targeted Lung Cancer Screening in High‐Risk Individuals in Australia
source_section: Summary of the Lung Cancer Screening and Assessment Pathway/Eligibility and Low‐Dose CT Scan Request/Suitability for Low‐Dose CT

breadcrumb: Summary of the Lung Cancer Screening and Assessment Pathway/Eligibility and Low‐Dose CT Scan Request/Suitability for Low‐Dose CT
recommendation_text: Reasons people may be unsuitable for low‐dose CT include weight restrictions of scanners, being unable to lie flat for a minimum of 5 min, having a symptomatic lung infection within the previous 12 weeks or having undergone a full chest CT scan within the previous 12 months or having one planned in the next 3 months.
source_name: Program Guidelines for the National Lung Cancer Screening Program: Targeted Lung Cancer Screening in High‐Risk Individuals in Australia
source_section: Summary of the Lung Cancer Screening and Assessment Pathway/Eligibility and Low‐Dose CT Scan Request/Suitability for Low‐Dose CT

recommendation_text: Practice points guide timely reassessment of suitability for low‐dose CT if an eligible person is temporarily unsuitable for screening.
source_name: Program Guidelines for the National Lung Cancer Screening Program: Targeted Lung Cancer Screening in High‐Risk Individuals in Australia
source_section: Summary of the Lung Cancer Screening and Assessment Pathway/Eligibility and Low‐Dose CT Scan Request/Suitability for Low‐Dose CT

recommendation_text: Shared decision‐making enables people to make an informed choice about lung cancer screening and is an integral component of the Program. Healthcare providers should support people to make an informed choice about lung cancer screening, even if they decide not to take part.

recommendation_text: Discussions about the Program should be inclusive and tailored to each individual's and their families' values, preferences, circumstances and information needs. recommendation_text: Consistent with the Australian Health Practitioner Regulation Agency cultural safety regulations, health professionals are required to create environments where Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples feel respected, valued and safe to engage in lung screening programs [42].

recommendation_text: Healthcare providers are responsible for sending the NCSR participant enrolment information through NCSR forms. Practice staff and nurses can be given delegate access to fill in these forms. Individuals can choose to opt out of the NCSR and still have a free low‐dose CT scan.

recommendation_text: In such cases, radiologists will still be able to receive the Medicare rebate, and requesting practitioners will be responsible for notifying patients of repeat or interval scans. recommendation_text: Requesting practitioners are required to complete a low‐dose CT request. The Program‐specific request form [43] is preferred, but requesting practitioners can use a usual practice form for radiology imaging requests.

recommendation_text: If using a usual practice form, the low‐dose CT scan request must identify that it is for lung cancer screening and include family history of lung cancer in any first‐degree relative (i. e. , parent, sibling or child), details of any previous chest CT scan (if known) and history of any cancer.

recommendation_text: This is required to ensure the patient is bulk‐billed for the scan and that the radiologist reads and reports on the scans using the Program's nodule management protocol. A new low‐dose CT scan request is needed for every scan.

recommendation_text: Participants should be advised when to book a low‐dose CT scan appointment—either as soon as possible (at Program entry) or as close to the required screening timepoint as possible.

recommendation_text: Low‐dose CT scans for the Program are available through public, private and mobile [44] radiology services, with participation open to all radiology services. Two MBS items [45] cover low‐dose CT scans under the program: the screening low‐dose CT scans undertaken at baseline and every 2 years (Item 57,410);
source_name: Program Guidelines for the National Lung Cancer Screening Program: Targeted Lung Cancer Screening in High‐Risk Individuals in Australia

recommendation_text: Structured radiology reporting ensures radiologists accurately and consistently report Program low‐dose CT scan results. Low‐dose CT scan reports are sent to the NCSR, and it is mandatory for radiologists to report within 30 days of performing a scan.

recommendation_text: Radiologists should record actionable additional findings alongside the scan outcome category in the structured clinical radiology report.
source_name: Program Guidelines for the National Lung Cancer Screening Program: Targeted Lung Cancer Screening in High‐Risk Individuals in Australia

breadcrumb: Summary of the Lung Cancer Screening and Assessment Pathway/Results and Next Steps/Actionable Additional Findings
recommendation_text: Requesting practitioners will be informed of actionable additional findings, with further recommended action required and will be responsible for managing these findings according to relevant clinical guidelines and best practice.
source_name: Program Guidelines for the National Lung Cancer Screening Program: Targeted Lung Cancer Screening in High‐Risk Individuals in Australia
source_section: Summary of the Lung Cancer Screening and Assessment Pathway/Results and Next Steps/Actionable Additional Findings

breadcrumb: Summary of the Lung Cancer Screening and Assessment Pathway/Results and Next Steps/Results Communication
recommendation_text: Requesting practitioners are responsible for communicating screening results to participants. Participants without a regular general practitioner may nominate an alternative recipient for their communication. The NCSR supports the process of results communication through direct correspondence to participants and requesting practitioners.
source_name: Program Guidelines for the National Lung Cancer Screening Program: Targeted Lung Cancer Screening in High‐Risk Individuals in Australia
source_section: Summary of the Lung Cancer Screening and Assessment Pathway/Results and Next Steps/Results Communication

breadcrumb: Summary of the Lung Cancer Screening and Assessment Pathway/Results and Next Steps/Results Communication
recommendation_text: The NCSR will notify participants registered with the NCSR and their requesting practitioners when results are available. NCSR communication does not replace duty of care responsibilities that healthcare providers have for communicating with and managing participant results.
source_name: Program Guidelines for the National Lung Cancer Screening Program: Targeted Lung Cancer Screening in High‐Risk Individuals in Australia
source_section: Summary of the Lung Cancer Screening and Assessment Pathway/Results and Next Steps/Results Communication

breadcrumb: Summary of the Lung Cancer Screening and Assessment Pathway/Results and Next Steps/Results Communication
recommendation_text: If a participant opts out of communication with the NCSR, the requesting practitioner will be responsible for all communication of results. Healthcare providers are to accommodate participants' communication preferences regarding how and when is appropriate to discuss their results and ensure culturally safe care.
source_name: Program Guidelines for the National Lung Cancer Screening Program: Targeted Lung Cancer Screening in High‐Risk Individuals in Australia
source_section: Summary of the Lung Cancer Screening and Assessment Pathway/Results and Next Steps/Results Communication

breadcrumb: Summary of the Lung Cancer Screening and Assessment Pathway/Results and Next Steps/Results Communication
recommendation_text: Practice points emphasise communicating results in a sensitive, clear and culturally safe manner to help participants understand their results and access appropriate psychosocial and smoking cessation supports.
source_name: Program Guidelines for the National Lung Cancer Screening Program: Targeted Lung Cancer Screening in High‐Risk Individuals in Australia
source_section: Summary of the Lung Cancer Screening and Assessment Pathway/Results and Next Steps/Results Communication

breadcrumb: Summary of the Lung Cancer Screening and Assessment Pathway/Results and Next Steps/Screening Reminders
recommendation_text: The NCSR will issue screening reminders for 2‐yearly and interval scans directly to participants and requesting practitioners. Healthcare providers are encouraged to send tailored reminders to participants whose participation is recorded in their EMR system.
source_name: Program Guidelines for the National Lung Cancer Screening Program: Targeted Lung Cancer Screening in High‐Risk Individuals in Australia
source_section: Summary of the Lung Cancer Screening and Assessment Pathway/Results and Next Steps/Screening Reminders

breadcrumb: Summary of the Lung Cancer Screening and Assessment Pathway/Results and Next Steps/Screening Reminders
recommendation_text: Requesting practitioners are responsible for sending screening reminders and follow‐up notifications to participants who have opted out of NCSR communication.
source_name: Program Guidelines for the National Lung Cancer Screening Program: Targeted Lung Cancer Screening in High‐Risk Individuals in Australia
source_section: Summary of the Lung Cancer Screening and Assessment Pathway/Results and Next Steps/Screening Reminders

breadcrumb: Summary of the Lung Cancer Screening and Assessment Pathway/Results and Next Steps/Program Exit and Re‐Entry
recommendation_text: Participants may exit the Program upon reaching its upper age limit of 71 years of age (age ineligibility), having a lung cancer diagnosis, becoming unable to undergo a low‐dose CT scan or actively opting out of the Program.
source_name: Program Guidelines for the National Lung Cancer Screening Program: Targeted Lung Cancer Screening in High‐Risk Individuals in Australia
source_section: Summary of the Lung Cancer Screening and Assessment Pathway/Results and Next Steps/Program Exit and Re‐Entry

breadcrumb: Summary of the Lung Cancer Screening and Assessment Pathway/Results and Next Steps/Program Exit and Re‐Entry
recommendation_text: Upon Program exit, participants' existing information will remain in the NCSR but participants will not receive further communications. Eligible participants may re‐enter the Program, including those successfully treated for lung cancer, where clinical judgement deems it appropriate.
source_name: Program Guidelines for the National Lung Cancer Screening Program: Targeted Lung Cancer Screening in High‐Risk Individuals in Australia
source_section: Summary of the Lung Cancer Screening and Assessment Pathway/Results and Next Steps/Program Exit and Re‐Entry

breadcrumb: Summary of the Lung Cancer Screening and Assessment Pathway/Results and Next Steps/Program Exit and Re‐Entry
recommendation_text: Healthcare providers should discuss broader options for managing any concerns about lung health with participants who have turned 71 years of age and exited the program.
source_name: Program Guidelines for the National Lung Cancer Screening Program: Targeted Lung Cancer Screening in High‐Risk Individuals in Australia
source_section: Summary of the Lung Cancer Screening and Assessment Pathway/Results and Next Steps/Program Exit and Re‐Entry

breadcrumb: Conclusion
recommendation_text: Lung cancer screening saves lives by helping to detect cancer at an earlier, treatable stage. The National Lung Cancer Screening Program's guidelines provide step‐by‐step guidance for clinical delivery and Program navigation, supporting healthcare providers to deliver the Program safely and effectively.
source_name: Program Guidelines for the National Lung Cancer Screening Program: Targeted Lung Cancer Screening in High‐Risk Individuals in Australia
source_section: Conclusion

breadcrumb: Conclusion
recommendation_text: The recommendations and practice points detailed in the Program's guidelines are grounded in best practice evidence and were developed in consultation with experts, consumers and the public to ensure the delivery of a culturally safe and equitable program for the Australian community.
